adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/utils/sync.py:136 — Always sending the new assignment_source_dict kwarg makes every task published by new code fail on old workers during a rolling deploy, dropping outbound assignment synchronization after retries

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async is now called with a new kwarg 'assignment_source_dict' (lines 137-143 in sync.py). During a rolling deploy, old workers that don't have the updated sync_assignee_outbound task signature would receive this new kwarg and fail because the old function definition doesn't accept 'assignment_source_dict'. The old signature only accepts (external_issue_id, user_id, assign) without the new parameter. This is a real backward compatibility issue during deployments.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/tasks/sync_assignee_outbound.py:56 — The task applies its captured assignee without comparing provenance time or current group state, so out-of-order workers can overwrite a newer cross-system assignment with stale data

adjudication.rationale: The finding points to a real architectural concern. The diff adds an AssignmentSource with a 'queued' timestamp field, but the sync_assignee_outbound task at line 56 (installation.sync_assignee_outbound call) doesn't use this timestamp to compare against current group state or handle out-of-order task execution. The diff shows the timestamp is captured but never used for ordering/comparison. However, this is more of a design limitation or potential race condition concern rather than a definitive bug - the code will function, but may have edge cases with concurrent updates. The finding is grounded in the diff but represents an incomplete implementation rather than a clear defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/tasks/sync_assignee_outbound.py:53 — Malformed nonempty provenance is silently converted to None and therefore fails open, re-enabling synchronization back to the source integration and defeating cycle prevention

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that in sync_assignee_outbound.py at line 53, when AssignmentSource.from_dict() returns None due to malformed input (as shown in the from_dict implementation that returns None on ValueError/TypeError), the code continues with parsed_assignment_source=None. This None value is then passed to should_sync(), which has the check 'if sync_source and sync_source.integration_id == self.org_integration.integration_id: return False'. When sync_source is None, this check is skipped, allowing synchronization to proceed even when the original intent was to prevent a sync cycle. This is a fail-open behavior that could defeat the cycle prevention mechanism.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py:18 — timezone.now is evaluated once at module import, so every source created by a worker shares a stale queued timestamp and cannot reliably support ordering or expiry checks
matched_golden_ids: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both comments identify the same issue: timezone.now() is evaluated once at class/module definition time rather than at instance creation time, causing all instances to share the same stale datetime value. adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/utils/sync.py:141 — Always emitting the new task keyword breaks rolling-version compatibility because pre-change workers reject assignment_source_dict as an unexpected argument.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async is now always called with 'assignment_source_dict' in kwargs (line 141), even when it's None. The task function signature at line 30-35 shows the new parameter was added with a default value. During rolling deployments, older workers that don't have this parameter in their task definition would receive this unexpected keyword argument and fail. This is a real compatibility issue for distributed systems with rolling deployments.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/tasks/sync_assignee_outbound.py:56 — Passing a second positional argument to the overridable should_sync hook breaks integrations that implement its prior one-argument contract.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that passing a second positional argument breaks integrations implementing the prior one-argument contract. However, looking at the diff, the `should_sync` method signature is changed to `should_sync(self, attribute: str, sync_source: AssignmentSource | None = None)` with a default value of `None`. This means the second argument is optional with a default, so existing implementations that only accept one argument would still work when called with just one argument. Additionally, the call at line 56 passes `parsed_assignment_source` which could be `None`, and the method signature accepts `None` as a valid value. The change is backward compatible because the new parameter has a default value.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py:18 — The serialized queued field uses an import-time default, so every AssignmentSource created by a long-lived process exposes the same stale timestamp.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` as a default value in the dataclass definition at line 18. In Python, default values are evaluated once at class definition time (import time), not at instance creation time. This means all instances of AssignmentSource created without explicitly passing a `queued` parameter will share the same timestamp from when the module was first imported. This is a known Python gotcha with mutable/callable defaults in dataclasses. The correct fix would be to use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py:18 — The eager `timezone.now()` default gives every source created in a worker the same import-time timestamp, so queued ordering cannot represent the actual assignment event.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` as a default value in the dataclass definition at line 18. In Python, default values are evaluated once at class definition time, not at instance creation time. This means all instances of AssignmentSource created without explicitly passing a `queued` parameter will share the same timestamp from when the module was first imported. This is a real bug that would cause incorrect timestamps for tracking when assignments were queued.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/models/groupassignee.py:138 — GroupAssigneeManager now exposes an integration-layer AssignmentSource in its public model API, coupling core assignment persistence to issue-sync transport concerns.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the GroupAssigneeManager.assign() and deassign() methods now accept an AssignmentSource parameter, which is defined in the integrations layer (sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py). This creates a coupling where the core model layer (groupassignee.py) depends on an integration-specific concept. This is a legitimate architectural concern - the model layer is now aware of integration-specific transport/sync concerns. The diff clearly shows this: line 138 adds 'assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None' to the assign method signature, and the import is added at line 15. This is a valid scope/architecture concern grounded in specific code changes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/mixins/issues.py:402 — The assignee provenance argument is hidden in untyped kwargs while the explicit parameter is added to the unrelated status-sync method, leaving implementations without a checked assignee-sync contract.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims the assignee provenance argument is hidden in untyped kwargs while assignment_source is added to sync_status_outbound. Looking at the diff, sync_assignee_outbound at line 402 already has assignment_source as an explicit parameter (line 59 in the task file shows it's passed explicitly). The abstract method sync_assignee_outbound in the mixin is not shown being modified in this diff - only sync_status_outbound is shown. The finding misreads the code: the implementation in sync_assignee_outbound.py correctly passes assignment_source as a named parameter to installation.sync_assignee_outbound(), not hidden in kwargs.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py:31 — The queue-boundary parser accepts dict values of Any and performs no runtime field validation, allowing invalid AssignmentSource instances to cross the task boundary.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims the parser performs 'no runtime field validation', but looking at the code in lines 29-34, the from_dict method uses `cls(**input_dict)` which will raise TypeError if required fields are missing or have wrong types (since AssignmentSource is a dataclass with typed fields). The try/except block catches ValueError and TypeError, returning None for invalid inputs. This IS validation - invalid data returns None rather than creating an invalid instance. The code handles the case appropriately by returning None for malformed input.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py:16 — source_name and queued are serialized through every outbound task but are never read by production code, adding dead payload and API surface.

adjudication.rationale: The finding is accurate. Looking at the diff, AssignmentSource has three fields: source_name, integration_id, and queued. The to_dict() method serializes all fields via asdict(), and this is passed through sync_assignee_outbound task. However, examining the production code paths: should_sync() only uses integration_id for comparison, and sync_assignee_outbound() only passes the source to should_sync() and sync_assignee_outbound(). The source_name and queued fields are indeed serialized but never read in the shown production code. This is a valid concern about unnecessary API surface/payload, though it could be argued these fields might be useful for debugging/logging purposes not shown in this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py:18 — queued is evaluated once at module import, so every later event from the worker carries the same stale timestamp and cannot support reliable ordering.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a bug in the dataclass definition. Line 18 shows `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` as a default value. In Python, default values for dataclass fields are evaluated once at class definition time (module import), not at instance creation time. This means all AssignmentSource instances will share the same timestamp from when the module was first imported, making the timestamp useless for ordering or tracking when assignments actually occurred. This is a well-known Python gotcha with mutable/callable defaults.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/tasks/sync_assignee_outbound.py:53 — A malformed nonempty source payload is silently treated as no source, disabling the cycle guard and allowing an update to be sent back to its originating integration.

adjudication.rationale: The finding is accurate. In sync_assignee_outbound.py lines 53-55, when assignment_source_dict is provided but malformed, AssignmentSource.from_dict() returns None (as shown in the new file at lines 30-34). This None value is then passed to should_sync(), which means the cycle guard check at lines 388-389 in issues.py (checking if sync_source.integration_id matches) will be skipped because sync_source is None. This allows the outbound sync to proceed even when the original source was the same integration, potentially causing sync cycles. A malformed but non-empty dict silently bypasses the protection.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/models/test_groupassignee.py:215 — The new test manually injects AssignmentSource and links only the source integration, so no test proves that real inbound assign or deassign events propagate to a different linked integration while suppressing the origin.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a gap in test coverage. The new test at line 215 (test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration) only tests that sync is suppressed when the source integration matches the target. However, there's no test demonstrating the positive case: that when an inbound assignment comes from integration A, it still propagates outbound to a different linked integration B. This is a valid test coverage concern for the new sync-cycle prevention logic, as the code comment at line 385-387 explicitly states 'This should still allow other integrations to propagate changes outward' but no test verifies this behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/integrations/services/test_assignment_source.py:36 — Checking only that queued is non-null misses that timezone.now() is evaluated once at import, causing every default AssignmentSource to share the same stale timestamp.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a real bug in the AssignmentSource dataclass. Looking at line 17 in src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` - this is a mutable default value that gets evaluated once at class definition time, not at instance creation time. This means all AssignmentSource instances created without explicitly passing a queued parameter will share the same timestamp from when the module was first imported. This is a well-known Python gotcha with mutable/callable defaults in dataclasses. The test at line 36 only checks `assert result.get('queued') is not None` which doesn't catch this bug - it would pass even though the timestamp is stale.
